heading: Places that carry the name
lead: You asked whether there is a street in Venice called *dei Franceschi*, and a Defranceschi bridge in Rijeka. There is a street, and it is better than expected. There is no bridge — there is something bigger.

rows.lab: Venice — Rio Terà dei Franceschi, at Santi Apostoli
rows.text:
It exists, it is in Cannaregio, and Giuseppe Tassini — whose *Curiosità veneziane* of 1872 is still the authority on where Venetian street names come from — explains it in full.

«**FRANCESCHI (Rio terrà dei) a' SS. Apostoli.** La denominazione di questo Rivo, il quale, prima del suo interramento, era attraversato da un piccolo ponte, **pur esso detto dei Franceschi**, ricorda quella **famiglia cittadinesca Franceschi**, la quale faceva per arma **un leone rampante col motto: *Sero sapimus*.**»

The name of this rio — which, before it was filled in, was crossed by a small bridge **also called dei Franceschi** — recalls that **citizen family Franceschi**, whose arms were **a lion rampant with the motto «Sero sapimus»: we grow wise too late.**

So there was a **Ponte dei Franceschi in Venice**, and the street is what is left of it after the canal was filled.

rows.lab: And it is named for a man this site already has
rows.text:
Tassini goes on. A **Benda** of this family presented, at the *redecima* of **1514**, the schedule of her many goods, among them buildings in the contrada of Santi Apostoli. And «**anche Andrea Franceschi, Cancellier Grande, nipote ed uno degli eredi di essa Benda, notificò nel 1537 di possedere una casa da statio a S. Apostolo**» — Andrea Franceschi, **Grand Chancellor**, nephew and one of Benda's heirs, declared in 1537 that he owned a *casa da statio* at S. Apostolo.

**That is the Andrea already on this site** — Titian's friend, Grand Chancellor of the Republic. The street is named for his family's houses. Not our kin, and this archive has never claimed him; but the question «is there a street in Venice called dei Franceschi» turns out to have the same answer as «who is the man in the Titian».

rows.lab: Four things about Andrea that this archive did not have
rows.text:
Tassini's entry is the fullest short life of him anywhere. He was born in **1472** — the site has said 1473 — and died in **1551**. He was the son of **Piero Franceschi, *zogelier*** — a jeweller — **son of the late Bortolo *dalla seda***, of the silk trade. So the Grand Chancellor of Venice was **a jeweller's son and a silk merchant's grandson**, which is what *cittadini originari* actually means in practice.

In **1513 he travelled to Constantinople and to Cairo with the Republic's ambassadors**. He was for about **seven years librarian of the Marciana**. He was learned in Greek and Latin, a lover of music, and **a collector of medals**. Titian portrayed him twice.

The Cairo journey needs a note. This archive earlier **cleared** a study of the Venetian embassy to Cairo of 1512 as irrelevant, on the ground that its Andrea de' Franceschi was of Cividale di Belluno and a different family. Tassini puts *this* Andrea on that road in 1513. **One of the two readings is wrong and it may be ours.** Reopened.

rows.lab: Three more Venetian vignettes, from the same book
rows.text:
**1560** — a **Ferigo Franceschi** declares that he owns two-thirds of a house at San Nicolò, under a roof called *la Cha Matta*.

**1575** — the terrible plague of that year **broke out in the parish of San Marziale in the house of a Vincenzo Franceschi**, where a man from Trento, already infected, had been given lodging. Tassini reports it without comment; it is the sort of sentence a family would rather not find in a street-name dictionary.

**1586** — **Angelo di Franceschi, son of Girolamo, secretary of the Senate, was murdered by Carlo Zeno**, who also fired an arquebus at his brother-in-law in the palace at the Frari, and was beheaded on 29 March 1586.

rows.lab: Rijeka — not a bridge, a pier
rows.text:
There is no Defranceschi bridge in Rijeka, and this archive looked hard for one. **There is a De Franceschi *pier*** — «**De Franceschijev gat**», in the main harbour, and it is one of the more important pieces of ground in the city.

It was built as the **Mol Zichy**, named for the Hungarian counts, and it is on the Croatian maritime-heritage register as «Pristanište Zichy / De Francescijev gat»: **150 metres along the east side, 134 on the west, 80 across the south**, about six metres of water at the edge.

Two things happened on it. In **1882** the first building in Rijeka harbour to be constructed in iron and concrete — **warehouse 4**, designed 1881 — went up on this pier, probably to the design of the architect **Mate Glavan**. And on **30 August**, in the first years of electric light, **Károly Zipernowsky** — the inventor of the transformer, with Bláthy and Déri — lit **Gat Zichy and warehouses II and III with four lamps borrowed from the Torpedo Factory**. Two bulbs in the warehouse, two on the pier. **The first electric light in Rijeka was switched on standing on the De Franceschi pier.**

rows.lab: And nobody says which De Franceschi
rows.text: The heritage register gives the pier both names and no explanation. Rijeka renamed a great many Hungarian and Italian things after 1945, and the obvious candidates are all in this archive — **Carlo the historian**, whose family Kobler traced in the Fiume registers; **Ivan Defranceski**, political commissar in the Istrian partisans in 1943–45; or one of Kobler's three Fiume households of the name. **This archive will not guess.** The Rijeka city archive and the municipal street-naming records would settle it in an afternoon, and it is on the list.

**This page has been asking «any others?» since it was written. Here is one, and it is not a curiosity — it is an address people lived at.**

*Il Giornaletto di Pola* carries **«via Carlo Defranceschi»** in its classified columns over and over: *«Rivolgersi deposito birra Goess, via Carlo Defranceschi 3»*, rooms to let, a kitchen and two rooms, a ground-floor flat. **One hundred and ten issues** carry the street name between **3 January 1914** and **20 May 1919**, almost all of them in that one paper — which is what an ordinary working street looks like in a newspaper, as opposed to a monument.

**Pola named a street after him, and by 1914 it was simply where the beer depot was.** The city that did it is the one whose Italian paper had printed his obituary twenty-one years earlier; ANNO's run of the *Giornaletto* begins around 1914, so the naming is certainly older than the first mention and this archive cannot yet say how much older.

Found on 14 September 2026 while reading the paper for something else entirely — a sixteen-year-old Fernasar in a police report on the same page.

**And the obvious question went unasked for a day: does the paper carry the family as well as the address?** All one hundred and sixty-four issues that carry the name have now been read in full. One hundred and fifty-eight of them are the street. **Four of them are people** — a conscript taken in the levy of June 1914, a householder who gave two crowns to the Red Cross, a bride who paid for her own wedding notice, and a man of sixty-three from Fasana who put his fist through a glass door. See [the Giornaletto read end to end](/giornaletto/).

Those are the two this archive can document. Against them stand the things that are **not** landmarks of this name and get mistaken for them: the **Villa De Franceschi** at Seget near Umag, which is a house and this family's own; the **Stanzia De Franceschi** at Svetvinčenat, a farmstead that had already passed out of the family by 1820 and survives only as a cadastral name; and, in Carnia, the ordinary fact that half the graveyard at Gorto carries it. If you know of another — a school, a square, a ship — this archive would rather chase it than assume it does not exist.

rows.lab: Who was the De Franceschi of the pier? A day's work, and the best candidate got weaker
rows.text:
**28 September 2026. The question was asked properly for the first time, and the honest result is a candidate demoted.**

**What the pier turns out to be.** *The City of Rijeka's own account of the port's building puts it in a set: «**nasipavanjem zapadne obale izgrađeno je Istarsko, Bečko, Budimpeštansko i Praško pristanište te De Francheschijev i Visinov gat**» — by filling the western shore were built the **Istrian, Vienna, Budapest and Prague** wharves **and the De Franceschi and Visinov gats**, all to the designs of **Antal Hajnal**, chief engineer of the Hungarian royal office for the construction of the port of Rijeka.* **So the pier is Hungarian-era construction, and it sits in a row where every other name is a place and only two are people.** *(doc for the grouping. **⚠ The city's page does not say who either man was**, and this archive will not fill that in.)*

*A neighbouring date fixes the set in use: **warehouse 17 on the Visinov gat was built in 1906–07** to the design of **Ferenc Pfaff**. Seven of the twenty warehouses survive and are protected.*

**⚠ And the leading candidate got weaker today, not stronger.**

*This archive's best guess has been **[Ferencz Defranceschi](/rijeka/), «révkapitány» of the Fiume Maritime Authority**, pensioned 1857 on 42 years 10 months and 5 days of service. **The Hungarian directory of 1848 undoes the comfortable part of that reading**: in that year the **harbour captaincy at Fiume was held by «Kapitány Sgardelli Alajos»**, while **Defranceschi Ferencz was «Főnök» — head — of the quarantine institute at Martinšćica**. *(doc, Budapesti utasító 1848, p. 70.)*

**His «révkapitány» title appears only at his pensioning**, in the 1872 parliamentary schedule, under the heading «**Fiumei tengerészeti hatóság**» — *and that is **the employing authority for the whole Hungarian Littoral**, not a statement of where he was posted.* **So «port captain of Fiume» was an overread, and it is withdrawn as a description.** *What remains true: a Defranceschi in the maritime service of that authority, retiring in 1857.*

**The timing is awkward too.** *Hajnal's western-shore programme is decades after 1857. A pier can of course honour a dead man — but the intuition that carried this candidate, that he was the port official on the spot when the port was built, is simply not available.* **(He is not eliminated; he is no longer the comfortable answer.)**

**Searched and nil, with the terms named.** *On [Hungaricana](https://www.hungaricana.hu) — the Hungarian state paperwork where Fiume's officials actually live — **`"Defranceschi" móló` → 0**, **`"Defranceschi" gát` → 0**, **`"molo Defranceschi"` → 0**, **`"molo De Franceschi"` → 0**, **`"De Franceschi" móló` → 0**. **The controls pass**: `Defranceschi révkapitány` → 5 and `Defranceschi kikötő` → 1 on the same portal in the same minutes.* **So the Hungarian accounts, pension schedules and directories know the man and do not know the pier** — *which is what one would expect of a source that records salaries and not quaysides, and is therefore weak evidence about the naming, not strong.*

**Still unrun, and still the things that would settle it:** *the **Državni arhiv u Rijeci**; the city's quay-renaming decrees; and the Italian-era port plans of 1924–45. The [Lučka uprava](https://www.portauthority.hr/kronologija/) chronology was tried today and the server returned 520.*

**Later the same day — the Lučka uprava chronology, retried and read.** *It returned HTTP 520 to a fetcher twice; it loads in a browser.* **It is a nil for the question, and a clean one:** *the port authority's own «Luka kroz povijest», 1717 to 2025, **names no pier of the Hungarian era at all** — the first quay it names by name is **Orlandov gat**, in 2013.* **So the pier's name is not in the port's own public chronology**, and that route is now exhausted rather than untried.

**What it gives instead is a frame, and one date that matters.**
· **1855** — *«Započinju prvi radovi na izgradnji suvremene riječke luke premještanjem ušća Rječine u novo korito»* — the first works on the modern port.
· **1867** — *the great basin is begun as the Dual Monarchy is created and «Rijeka postaje glavna postaja za izlaz mađarskog gospodarstva u svijet»*. **This is the frame Hajnal's western-shore programme sits in**, and it opens **ten years after [Ferencz Defranceschi](/rijeka/) had already retired.**
· **⚠ 1941–45** — *«Njemačka vojska je prilikom povlačenja iz riječke luke **porušila sve vezove za prihvat brodova**, pretovarnu mehanizaciju i **više od 50% skladišnih kapaciteta**»* — **the German withdrawal destroyed every berth in the port**, and reconstruction followed in 1950.

**⚠ And that last date sharpens the question rather than settling it.** *A port rebuilt from destroyed berths is exactly when quays get renamed — and «**De Francescijev**» is a Croatian possessive, the form a **post-1945** naming would take. **Against that**: the City of Rijeka's own history attributes the *gat* name to Hajnal's Hungarian-era programme, decades earlier.* **The two accounts are not reconciled here, and neither is discarded.** *(Both doc; the inference from either is not made.)*

source_land: Venice: Giuseppe Tassini, «Curiosità veneziane, ovvero Origini delle denominazioni stradali di Venezia» (Venice, 1872 edition), the entry FRANCESCHI (Rio terrà dei), pp. 288–289, read from the Internet Archive scan; his own authorities are the «Cronaca di quarantasei famiglie di Cittadini Veneziani» (Biblioteca Marciana, Cl. VII, Cod. CCCXLI) and the «Memorie concernenti la Vita dei Veneti Cancellieri Grandi» (Cl. VII, Cod. CLXVI). Rijeka: the Croatian maritime-heritage register entry «Pristanište Zichy / De Francescijev gat»; and the Rijeka chronology at moja-rijeka.eu, citing Nana Palinić, «Povijesna skladišta riječke luke», in «Industrijska baština» I (2003), Pro torpedo, Rijeka 2005, p. 395.
